method: Web search to locate sources; text read via curl/pdftotext of publisher or author full text, OpenAlex abstract API, or WebFetch; DOIs confirmed against Crossref titles. Quotes copied from fetched text. 'not found' rows record named items without a sourced number.

rows.category: loss attribution (hazard vs exposure vs vulnerability)
rows.item: Drivers of the historical increase in weather-disaster losses
rows.quantity: Attribution of observed loss increase to exposure vs climate-driven hazard change
rows.value_text: qualitative: loss increase caused primarily by increasing exposure and value of capital at risk
rows.source: Bouwer (2011), Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society
rows.quote: The observed loss increase is caused primarily by increasing exposure and value of capital at risk.
rows.notes: Review of published normalization studies for weather hazards only; no seismic losses. Gives no percentage split. Shows that loss trends are dominated by exposure growth, which is itself poorly observed; does NOT show how much loss variance comes from exposure error in any single event model.

rows.category: loss attribution (hazard vs exposure vs vulnerability)
rows.outcome: fatalities and economic loss per exposed population/GDP (climate-related hazards)
rows.quantity: Factor by which global average mortality rate (fatalities/exposed population) dropped, 1980-1989 to 2007-2016
rows.value_text: dropped by 6.5 (mortality) and nearly 5 times (economic loss rate)
rows.quote: global average mortality and economic loss rates that have dropped by 6.5 and nearly 5 times, respectively, from 1980-1989 to 2007-2016
rows.notes: Vulnerability here is a residual (reported loss / modelled exposure), so it absorbs exposure-model and loss-reporting errors. Climate-related hazards only (floods, storms, etc.), not earthquakes. Economic-loss-rate factor 'nearly 5' is stated without a decimal value.

rows.category: loss attribution (hazard vs exposure vs vulnerability)
rows.item: Relative impact of hazard (demand) vs vulnerability (capacity) epistemic uncertainty on earthquake loss
rows.quantity: Which component dominates loss sensitivity
rows.value_text: qualitative: capacity (vulnerability) uncertainty larger than demand (ground motion) uncertainty for a single scenario
rows.source: Crowley et al. (2005), Earthquake Engineering & Structural Dynamics
rows.quote: the influence of the epistemic uncertainty in the capacity is larger than that of the demand for a single earthquake scenario
rows.notes: Single-scenario, single-region sensitivity study with a displacement-based loss method; no variance shares in the abstract. Exposure (building inventory) uncertainty not separated as its own component in the abstract.

rows.category: loss attribution (hazard vs exposure vs vulnerability)
rows.item: Variance-based sensitivity of portfolio loss epistemic uncertainty
rows.quantity: Ranking of eight uncertain inputs by contribution to epistemic uncertainty in AAL
rows.value_text: qualitative: ranking only; design level (an exposure attribute) first, then fragility functions, median ground motion, GMPE, structural type
rows.source: Markhvida et al. (2020), Proc. 17th World Conference on Earthquake Engineering (paper C000796)
rows.quote: the five most important variables according to both methods are building design level, fragility functions, median ground motion, ground motion prediction equations
rows.notes: Conference paper, no DOI. Sobol-type indices shown only in a figure; no percentage stated in text. Fictional portfolio, so the ranking is illustrative. Notable because the top variable is an exposure attribute (share of buildings per design level) that is rarely observed directly.

rows.category: loss attribution (hazard vs exposure vs vulnerability)
rows.item: Peer-reviewed percentage share of seismic loss variance attributable to exposure vs vulnerability vs hazard
rows.quantity: Variance share (%) by component
rows.value_text: not found
rows.notes: Searched for Crowley/Bommer, Silva (2016, doi 10.1080/13632469.2016.1138172), Porter et al., GEM and Kalakonas-type exposure-uncertainty studies (e.g. doi 10.1007/s10518-021-01312-9). Abstracts read give qualitative rankings or case-specific sensitivities, not a stated global percentage split. Do not cite a number for this.

rows.quantity: Deaths in ~100 continental-interior earthquakes with >=1,000 deaths (vs 800,000 at plate boundaries)
rows.value_text: at least 1,400,000 deaths (continental interiors) vs 800,000 (plate boundaries)
rows.quote: about 100 took place in continental interiors, causing at least 1,400,000 deaths, whereas earthquakes at plate boundaries caused 800,000 deaths
rows.notes: Commentary. Counts only ~130 earthquakes with >=1,000 deaths. Text says these events 'frequently take place on faults that were either previously unknown, or whose threat had not been recognized' but gives NO fraction of deaths on unmapped faults. A rebuttal (McCloskey 2011, Nature Geoscience, doi 10.1038/ngeo1221) argues the bigger problem is vulnerability on known faults.

rows.quantity: Surface rupture length on a previously unidentified fault
rows.value_text: 29.5 ± 0.5-km-long surface rupture
rows.quote: The earthquake occurred on a previously unidentified fault system and generated a 29.5 ± 0.5-km-long surface rupture
rows.notes: Single event. Crossref lists online date 2011-11; print 2012. Shows a Mw 7.1 source absent from fault maps; does not give a rate for such events.

rows.outcome: ground rupture; seismic hazard model completeness
rows.quantity: Number of major faults with surface rupture, along mapped and unmapped faults
rows.value_text: at least 12 major faults; rupture along both mapped and unmapped faults
rows.quote: The rupture propagated northward for more than 170 kilometers along both mapped and unmapped faults before continuing offshore
rows.notes: Abstract does not state how many of the 12 were unmapped. Litchfield et al. (2018, BSSA, doi 10.1785/0120170300) abstract says '>20' crustal faults ruptured, also without an unmapped count. A secondary search snippet attributed '11 previously unmapped faults' to an earlier 2016 reconnaissance report; NOT verified, not used as a value.

rows.item: Share of 2023 surface rupture on previously mapped faults
rows.quantity: Percent of rupture length on faults in pre-event active-fault maps
rows.value_text: not found (abstract states >500 km of rupture 'primarily' on the named East Anatolian (~345 km) and Cardak (~175 km) faults)
rows.source: Reitman et al. (2023), The Seismic Record
rows.quote: produced > 500 km of surface rupture primarily on the left-lateral East Anatolian (~345 km) and Çardak (~175 km) faults
rows.notes: Both main faults were named, mapped structures before 2023, so this event is a counter-example to the unmapped-fault story: losses were driven by known faults plus building vulnerability. No percentage on mapped vs unmapped splays found; search snippets mention a previously unmapped segment near Malatya (not verified).

rows.quantity: Share of total moment rate assigned off modelled faults (UCERF3 deformation models)
rows.value_text: between 32% and 37% (UCERF2-implied: 27%)
rows.source: Field et al. (2014), Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America 104(3)
rows.quote: In terms of the percentage of the total moment rate that is off-fault, the new deformation models have values between 32% and 37%
rows.notes: Paper states off-fault deformation 'occurs at least partially on unmodeled faults'. Moment-rate share, not loss or hazard share; off-fault values include aseismic processes. This is the closest sourced USGS-model figure to 'fraction of California hazard from unmapped faults'; it is NOT that fraction.

rows.quantity: Share of observed (smoothed) seismicity falling inside modelled fault zones
rows.value_text: 53% (UCERF3 smoothing, Fault Model 3.1) to 59% (Fault Model 3.2)
rows.source: Field et al. (2014), Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America 104(3)
rows.quote: 53% for UCERF3 smoothed seismicity paired with Fault Model 3.1
rows.notes: Range across four smoothing/fault-model combinations is 53%-59% as listed. Depends on fault-zone polygon widths. Applies to rates of all magnitudes in the smoothed catalog, not to large-earthquake hazard or loss.

rows.quantity: Share of UCERF2 faults with a measured slip rate
rows.value_text: Only about 30%
rows.source: Field et al. (2014), Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America 104(3)
rows.quote: Only about 30% of UCERF2 faults had measured slip rate estimates, and most of these had an estimate at only a single location.
rows.notes: Describes the predecessor model; UCERF3 added geodetic inversions. Shows that even mapped faults in the best-studied US region are mostly unobserved in rate.

rows.quantity: Number of faults compiled; share with slip-rate information
rows.value_text: ∼13,500 faults; about 77% with slip rate information
rows.quote: The GAF‐DB contains ∼13,500 faults, each with associated attributes
rows.notes: Abstract asserts 'Spatial completeness is high' without a quantitative completeness metric. The count measures compiled known faults, NOT completeness against true active faults; no global estimate of unmapped active faults found.

rows.outcome: tsunami and submarine landslide hazard modelling (bathymetry)
rows.quantity: Share of world ocean floor mapped to modern (direct-measurement) standards
rows.source: Nippon Foundation-GEBCO Seabed 2030 announcement, reported by Hellenic Shipping News
rows.quote: 28.7% of the world's ocean floor has now been mapped
rows.notes: Secondary reprint of the Seabed 2030 press release (21 April 2026, IHO Assembly). Earlier: 27.3% (GEBCO 2025 Grid), 24.9% (2023). Covers seafloor depth only; NOT sub-seafloor structure, sediment properties or fault mapping offshore.

rows.outcome: direct sampling depth of the crust
rows.quantity: Maximum depth of the deepest borehole
rows.quote: Kola superdeep well SG-3 reaches a depth of 12,262 m
rows.notes: Publisher page returned 403; number seen only in a search snippet of the abstract; widely repeated elsewhere. Crustal thickness at the site (often given as ~35-40 km) NOT sourced here, so no depth fraction is given. A point sample, not areal coverage.

rows.region: countries covering ~75% of global groundwater withdrawals
rows.item: In situ groundwater-level monitoring synthesized globally
rows.quantity: Number of monitoring wells analysed
rows.value_text: 170,000 monitoring wells and 1,693 aquifer systems
rows.quote: we analyse in situ groundwater-level trends for 170,000 monitoring wells and 1,693 aquifer systems in countries that encompass approximately 75% of global groundwater withdrawals
rows.notes: Abstract also says groundwater levels 'have not been synthesized at the global scale' before. A count of wells, NOT an areal coverage fraction; '75%' is share of withdrawals, not land area. Relevance to geohazard outcomes is indirect (subsidence).

rows.quantity: Share of US land mapped at 7.5-minute quadrangle detail (1989 poll of state surveys)
rows.value_text: Only 19.6 percent
rows.source: Soller & Berg (1997), Geotimes ('The National Geologic Map Database -- A Progress Report'), hosted by USGS NGMDB
rows.quote: Only 19.6 percent of the land in the United States had been mapped at that level of geologic detail.
rows.notes: Old figure. No current USGS percentage for 1:24,000 coverage found. Surface geology only.

rows.item: Geologic map coverage at adequate detail (NCGMP fact sheet)
rows.quantity: Share of conterminous US mapped at the 'appropriate level of detail'
rows.value_text: Less than 50 percent
rows.source: American Geosciences Institute (2018), Geoscience Currents fact sheet 'Geologic Mapping for the Nation: The NCGMP'
rows.quote: Less than 50 percent of the conterminous U.S. has been mapped at the appropriate level of detail for today’s challenges.
rows.notes: Value is an upper bound ('less than'), scale not stated in the sentence. Advocacy fact sheet, not peer-reviewed. A search summary attributed it to a 2010 coverage map; not verified.

rows.quantity: Share of global urban population living in centres with >80% OSM building completeness
rows.value_text: 1,848 urban centres (16% of the urban population) exceed 80%; 9,163 cities (48% of the urban population) below 20%
rows.quote: For 1,848 urban centres (16% of the urban population), OSM building footprint data exceeds 80% completeness
rows.notes: Completeness is itself a machine-learning estimate. Footprints only; NOT building height, material, age or structural system, which drive vulnerability. Urban only. Same paper: 48% of urban population in cities <20% complete.

rows.item: Urban population in slums or informal settlements (SDG 11.1.1)
rows.quantity: People living in slums or informal settlements
rows.value_text: an estimated 1.13 billion people
rows.source: UN Statistics Division (2026), SDG Extended Report 2026, Goal 11
rows.quote: with an estimated 1.13 billion people living in slums or informal settlements
rows.notes: A people count, NOT a building count and NOT a share of non-engineered buildings. Other UN-Habitat 2026 materials give 1.16 billion (24.8% of urban population, 2024); not verified here. No sourced global share of non-engineered buildings found.

rows.item: Number of countries with a national building inventory (vs. exposure inferred from census/housing statistics)
rows.quantity: Count of countries
rows.value_text: not found
rows.source: Yepes-Estrada et al. (2023), Earthquake Spectra (abstract only) and GEM exposure documentation
rows.notes: GEM global exposure model covers 215 countries and territories (GEM docs page, read) and is built 'bottom-up' from national statistics and local datasets; abstract mentions 'regions with large fractions of informal construction' but neither source states how many countries have a building-by-building inventory. Full paper not read (paywalled).

rows.item: Population exposure uncertainty from choice of gridded population dataset
rows.quantity: Total population exposed to the 100-year flood under LandScan, WorldPop and HRSL
rows.value_text: 134, 122, and 101 million (LandScan, WorldPop, HRSL); reduction up to ~60% in single countries
rows.quote: the total population exposed to the 100 year flood in the 18 countries was calculated to be 134, 122, and 101 million
rows.notes: Same hazard layer (~90 m inundation model), only population layer changes. Shows exposure uncertainty of ~1/3 between datasets for floods; NOT tested for earthquakes, and none of the layers is ground truth.

rows.outcome: economic loss and fatalities (EM-DAT natural-hazard events)
rows.quantity: Share of natural-hazard disaster events with missing total estimated damages
rows.value_text: missing for 96.2% (reconstruction costs), 88.1% (insured damages), 41.5% (total estimated damages); total deaths 1.3%
rows.quote: data were missing for 96.2% of disaster events on reconstruction costs, for 88.1% on insured damages and 41.5% on total estimated damages
rows.notes: Missingness predicted by year, country income group and disaster type, so not missing at random. EM-DAT inclusion thresholds (>=10 deaths, >=100 affected, etc.) already exclude small events. Death field near-complete (1.3% missing) but 60% of records report zero deaths.

rows.quantity: Share of EM-DAT entries with missing economic loss information
rows.value_text: 11143 entries ... 80.38% of the total
rows.source: CRED (2021), Cred Crunch No. 63 'Missing data on economic losses variables from EM-DAT'
rows.quote: 11143 entries had missing information regarding economic losses which amounts to 80.38% of the total.
rows.notes: Includes technological disasters and epidemics (100% missing), so higher than the natural-hazard-only figure of Jones et al. (2022, 41.5% for total damages). Kept as a separate row because the two disagree. Newsletter, not peer-reviewed.

rows.quantity: Underestimate of fatal landslide events by EM-DAT relative to a dedicated landslide database, 2004-2010
rows.value_text: underestimated the number of fatal landslide events by ∼ 2000 % and fatalities by 430 %
rows.source: Froude & Petley (2018), Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences (citing Petley 2012)
rows.quote: the EM-DAT database underestimated the number of fatal landslide events by ∼ 2000 % and fatalities by 430 %
rows.notes: Secondary statement of Petley (2012). Same paper cites a 2007-2013 comparison: ~1400% events, 331% fatalities. Global Fatal Landslide Database itself: 55,997 deaths in 4,862 non-seismic events 2004-2016, and may still 'underestimate the true level of loss by up to 15 %'. Excludes earthquake-triggered landslides.

rows.quantity: Number of stream gauges in the global database analysed
rows.value_text: 32,091 stream gauges
rows.quote: We used a global database of 32,091 stream gauges
rows.notes: Gauges sit disproportionately on large, perennial, human-dominated rivers; sparse on non-perennial rivers and in protected areas. Mapped onto ~3 million GRADES river segments (>25 km2 drainage); the paper does not state a single gauged fraction, so none is computed here.

rows.item: Decline of river gauging network / GRDC data availability
rows.quantity: Percent or count decline in reporting gauges
rows.value_text: not found (qualitative only: 'possible decline in network coverage')
rows.quote: these databases are at risk due to a possible decline in network coverage
rows.notes: Commentary; abstract gives no number. A quantitative GRDC decline figure was not located in this pass.

rows.item: Population with access to earthquake early warning
rows.quantity: People with access to EEW from traditional seismic networks (early 2021)
rows.value_text: 260 million people (plus ~150 million Android early-warning users in the first year)
rows.quote: bringing the total global population with access to EEW to 260 million people
rows.notes: Two-column PDF; quote reassembled across a hyphenated line break ('to-tal'). Access to alerts, NOT station density or ground-motion observation coverage; no denominator (exposed population) given in the text read.

rows.item: Share of population or seismic-hazard area within a given distance of a seismic or strong-motion station
rows.quantity: Percent within X km
rows.value_text: not found
rows.notes: No published global population-weighted station-distance statistic located. Would need to be computed (e.g. FDSN station inventory x gridded population); none computed here.
